heading: The Tragedy of the Commons / by Garrett Hardin
text:
The Tragedy of the Commons
by Garrett Hardin
Science, Dec. 13, 1968
vol. 162, pp. 1243-1248
• Tragedy for cattle herdsmen (Lloyd, 1833)
– 10 herdsmen each with 100 cattle; at sustainable limit of commons; 
if herdsman adds 1
• Increase individual benefit, but decrease shared resources
– Rational decision of each herdsman: keep adding animals
– Result: commons overgrazed and destroyed
• Growing pistachio trees in CA
– Pistachio needs lots of water
– Drought → pistachio price went up → grow more pistachio → 
drought more severe

heading: What is air pollution / • As defined in Florida Administrative Code:
text:
What is air pollution
• As defined in Florida Administrative Code:
• “Air pollution is the presence in the outside 
atmosphere … of any one or more substances 
or pollutants in quantities which are or may be 
harmful or injurious to human health or welfare, 
animal or plant life, or property, or unreasonably 
interfere with the enjoyment of life or property, 
including outdoor recreation.”

heading: Scales of air pollution problems / 6
text:
Scales of air pollution problems
6
• Personal
• Micro-environmental (meters) – indoor air pollution 
• Local (< 5 km) – hot spots, near source
• Urban (~ 50 km) – urban smog
• Regional (50 – 500 km) – acid deposition, visibility
• Continental (500 – 1000 km) – long-range 
transport, stratospheric ozone depletion
• Global – stratospheric ozone depletion, long range 
transport, climate change

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 18
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
18
• 1960s: Social change and significant national 
environmental movements
– Sierra Club, Wilderness Society
– 1962: Rachel Carson’s ‘Silent Spring’ 
• 1963: Clean Air Act (CAA)
– Broadened federal role in air quality management
• Grants for program development/improvement of state and local air 
pollution control
• Research, training, and technical assistance
• Federal enforcement authority for interstate air pollution problems
• Federal research responsibility for automobile and SOx pollution
• Authority to compile and publish criteria for pollutants

text:

19
• 1965: Motor Vehicle Air Pollution Control Act
– Amendment to 1963 CAA
– Established the National Air Pollution Control 
Administration (NAPCA)
– Authorized DHEW/NAPCA to promulgate motor 
vehicle emissions standards

text:

control technique info
– States to develop state air quality standards, state 
implementation plan (SIP)

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 24
text:

• 1990: Clean Air Act Amendments

heading: CAPs & HAPs / • 6 Criteria Air Pollutants (CAPs):
text:
CAPs & HAPs
• 6 Criteria Air Pollutants (CAPs):
– O3, CO, NO2, SO2, Pb, PM (PM2.5 & PM10)
– Concentration level set in NAAQS (in CAA)
– Ubiquitous, most harmful to health and environment
• 189 Hazardous Air Pollutants (HAPs)
– A.K.A. toxic air pollutants or air toxics
– Known/suspected to cause cancer, or other serious 
health or environmental effects
– Goal: reduce emissions (NESHAPS)
– Primary, man-made emissions dominates
8

heading: Particulate Matter (PM) / • A.K.A. aerosol, can be a solid/liquid/mixed
text:
Particulate Matter (PM)
• A.K.A. aerosol, can be a solid/liquid/mixed
• PM10 & PM2.5
– PMs with aerodynamic diameter < 10 or 2.5 µm
• 1 µm =  1x10-6 m
– Can lodge in airway once inhaled. 
– PM2.5 penetrate deep into lungs (alveoli region)
• Many emission sources
– Fire, dust, agriculture, fuel combustion, cars etc…
– Both primary/secondary, natural/man-made sources
• Secondary organic aerosol (SOA) is a major research topic
9

heading: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2) / • Usually NO and NO2 are measured together
text:
Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2)
• Usually NO and NO2 are measured together
– NO eventually oxidized to NO2
– NO + NO2 = NOx (different from NOy and NOz!)
• NOz = a combination of several reactive nitrogen species
• NOy = NOx + NOz
• Mostly man-made, primary emissions (fuel 
combustion at high temperatures)
– Mobile source, power plants dominates
• Some natural sources
– Lighting generate NOx
– Some plants also emit NOx 10

heading: Ground-level ozone (O3) / • One major component of photochemical smog
text:
Ground-level ozone (O3)
• One major component of photochemical smog
• Ground-level O3 BAD; stratospheric O3 GOOD.
– Health effect when exposed near ground
– Stratospheric O3 layer absorbs harmful UV
• Secondary pollutants, negligible direct emissions 
– Primarily from NOX and VOC, mixing with sunlight
– VOC: Volatile Organic Compounds
• From evaporation of organic solvents, incomplete combustion etc…
• Trees emits VOC (biogenic): mostly isoprene
• Globally, trees emits more VOC than man-made sources
• Ronald Reagan (1981): Trees cause more pollution than 
automobiles do
11

heading: Sulfur Dioxide (SO2) / • From combustion of sulfur-containing fuel
text:
Sulfur Dioxide (SO2)
• From combustion of sulfur-containing fuel
• Primary, anthropogenic sources dominate
– Coal fire power plants is the biggest source
– Also industry, mobile, fire (wild + prescribed)
– Some natural source: sulfur springs
• Major contributor to acid rain, especially 
northeastern US
12

heading: Carbon Monoxide (CO) / • Colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas
text:
Carbon Monoxide (CO)
• Colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas
• Mostly primary, from incomplete fuel combustion
– Mobile source, fire are the biggest ones
• Some plants emits CO (biogenic)
• CO binds with hemoglobin, reduce oxygen 
carrying capacity of blood
13

heading: Lead (Pb) / • Particulate lead
text:
Lead (Pb)
• Particulate lead
• Combustion of fuels with lead additives
• Leaded gas phased out → lead in ambient air 
decreased by 99%
– Leaded gas invented by Thomas Midgley Jr. who also 
brought us Freon (CFC)
• Lead particularly toxic to children
• Houses built before 1978 has lead paint

heading: Air Pollution Health Effects / • Effects on human

Air Pollution Health Effects

– Numerous adverse health effects, ranging from minor 
irritation, discomfort, to chest pain, asthma, birth 
defect, cancer and death

– Eutrophication (excessive nutrition, e.g. nitrogen)
– Damage ozone layer → increase harmful UV radiation
– Numerous others….

insoluble, relatively inert

heading: Stratospheric ozone chemistry - CFCs / 24
text:
Stratospheric ozone chemistry - CFCs
24
• In stratosphere, CFC break down when exposed 
to far-UV, release ClOx and atomic chlorine
• CFC don’t break down in troposphere (why?)
– Hence climb to stratosphere
• Destruct ozone through the generalized catalytic 
ozone destruction mechanism
Cl + O3 → ClO + O2
ClO + O → Cl + O2
NET:        O + O₃ → 2O₂
active chlorine

heading: Stratospheric ozone chemistry - CFCs / 25
text:
Stratospheric ozone chemistry - CFCs

• -Cl chain length: 10 -1,000 (Jacobson, 2002)
– One Cl molecule on average destructs 10-1,000 
ozone molecules in lower and upper stratosphere, 
respectively. Aka chain length
– Bigger chain length number, more powerful ozone 
destruction
• -Br chain length: 100 - 10,000 (Jacobson, 2002)
– Slower reaction, more efficient
• The estimated numbers vary

heading: Stratospheric ozone chemistry - CFCs / 26
text:
Stratospheric ozone chemistry - CFCs
26
• Sink of active chlorine (Cl, ClO)
– Reactions to form reservoir species: HCl and ClONO2
• Hydrochloric acid and chlorine nitrate
– Temporarily store chlorine
– When sunlight present, can photolyzed back to free 
chlorine, continue ozone destruction
• Bromine chemistry is similar

heading: Ozone depletion process / 30
text:
Ozone depletion process

• During polar night (before spring)
– Polar stratospheric clouds (PSC) forms → reactions 
occur inside PSC → convert inactive Cl/Br (such as 
reservoir species HCl and ClONO2) to species that 
are photo-chemically active (Cl2, HOCl, ClNO2 etc)
– Chlorine activation
• Beginning of polar day (early spring)
– Photo-chemically active species go through 
photolysis reaction → release active Cl/Br (Cl, ClO) → 
catalytically destroy ozone

heading: Climate Variability and Climate Change / • Climate Variability: The range of fluctuations around long-term
text:
Climate Variability and Climate Change
• Climate Variability: The range of fluctuations around long-term 
average climate conditions. It refers to variations in the state of 
climate beyond that of individual weather events.
– Drivers of climate variability include El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and 
other phenomena. They produce warm, cool, wet, or dry periods across different 
regions and are a natural part of climate variability.
• Climate Change: A significant and persistent change in the mean 
state of the climate or its variability. Climate change occurs in 
response to changes in some aspect of Earth’s environment.
– It can include changes in temperature, precipitation, increase in occurrence of 
extreme weather events, as well as increased/decreased variability.

Topics
• Introduction to air quality models

heading: To start with….. / 3
text:
To start with…..
3
• What is a model?
– A representation of a system
• To investigate its properties and/or perform predictions
– Vary substantially in complexity
• Why we need model in air quality field?
– Measurements are expensive
– Measurements are limited, spatially and temporally
– Need to answer “what if” questions

heading: To start with….. / 4
text:
To start with…..
4
• “all models are wrong”, but useful
• There are always errors and biases in 
model outputs
• Caution must be taken to evaluate model 
outputs, and to identify and correct biases 
and errors

heading: Atmospheric science
text: Atmospheric science

heading: Overview / • Mean to, mechanistically, mathematically
text:
Overview
• Mean to, mechanistically, mathematically 
approximate actual physical chemical process in 
the atmosphere
– Not a strict definition
• Use model to investigate the fate and transport 
of chemical species in the atmosphere
– Note that this is for air quality purposes
– Many advanced models include more than just 
atmosphere, and are capable of more purposes

heading: A simplified overview / • Eulerian vs Lagrangian
text:
A simplified overview
• Eulerian vs Lagrangian
• Roughly models can be categorized as
– Box model
– Gaussian type models
– Chemical transport model (CTM)
– Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models
– Special purpose models
• No strict categorizations

heading: Lagrangian vs Eulerian approach / 8
text:
Lagrangian vs Eulerian approach
8
• Two basic approaches to model pollutant transport
• Lagrangian: Focus on one ‘piece’ of pollutant, track it 
through space and time (stalker)
• Eulerian: Focus on the same area, estimate spatial 
concentrations distributions at each time step (snapshot)

– Can be very complex (e.g.

• Treat entire study

assume instantaneous

• Still widely used to study

heading: Gaussian models / • Steady-state vs non-steady-state models
text:
Gaussian models
• Steady-state vs non-steady-state models
• Steady-state
– Assume homogeneous meteorological fields
– Usually no “memory” effects
• Non-steady-state
– Spatially varying meteorological fields
– “Remembers” concentration from previous time-step 
(usually hour)

Steady-state Gaussian plume models
11
• Longest history in regulatory air quality modeling
• Use Gaussian plume models
• Assume homogeneous meteorological condition
• Example models

– ADMS-URBAN

text:
Non-steady state Gaussian models
12
• Pollutant modeled as “puff” or “particles”
• Movements of “puff” or “particles” are tracked 
spatially and temporally at each time step
– Normally using 3-D meteorological field data from 
weather forecasting models
• Mainly applied in urban scale
– Can be applied for regional scale
• Long range transportation

heading: Eulerian chemical transport models / 16
text:
Eulerian chemical transport models
16
• Discretize the study area into grid cells
• Do not try to solve for meteorological fields
– Data from weather forecasting models (e.g. WRF)
• At each time step
– Solve for pollutant concentrations in each cell 
altogether from groups of mass balance equations
– Homogeneous concentration distribution within cell
• Example: CMAQ, CAMx, UCD
• Generally applied in large scale, from regional 
scale (e.g. Eastern US) to global

heading: Eulerian chemical transport models / 17
text:
Eulerian chemical transport models
17
• Pros:
– Detailed and comprehensive chemistry
– Can be applied for large scale modeling
– Able to include unlimited number of emission sources
• Cons:
– Steep learning curve
– Computational expensive
– No concentration variation within grid cell
• Can be achieved with certain techniques

heading: Computational fluid dynamics models / 18
text:
Computational fluid dynamics models
18
• Virtually all use Eulerian approach
• Solve for meteorological field and concentrations 
at the same time
• Generally applied from continental to global 
scale
• Examples: GEOS-CHEM, WRF-CHEM, 
GATOR-GCMOM etc…..

heading: Computational fluid dynamics models / 19
text:
Computational fluid dynamics models
19
• Pros:
– No need to run weather forecasting models 
separately
– Detailed and comprehensive chemistry
– Unlimited number of emission sources
• Cons:
– Even more computational expensive
– Steeper learning curve
– No concentration variation within grid cell

heading: Special purpose models / 20
text:
Special purpose models
20
• Models designed for specific applications
• Models use traditional fluid dynamics model
– E.g.: CTAG
– Characterize small-scale turbulence
– Very high spatial resolution (down to meter scale)
– Very computational expensive

heading: What is air pollution / • As defined in Florida Administrative Code:
text:
What is air pollution
• As defined in Florida Administrative Code:
• “Air pollution is the presence in the outside 
atmosphere … of any one or more substances 
or pollutants in quantities which are or may be 
harmful or injurious to human health or welfare, 
animal or plant life, or property, or unreasonably 
interfere with the enjoyment of life or property, 
including outdoor recreation.”

heading: Scales of air pollution problems / 5
text:
Scales of air pollution problems
5
• Personal
• Micro-environmental (meters) – indoor air pollution 
• Local (< 5 km) – hot spots, near source
• Urban (~ 50 km) – urban smog
• Regional (50 – 500 km) – acid deposition, visibility
• Continental (500 – 1000 km) – long-range 
transport, stratospheric ozone depletion
• Global – stratospheric ozone depletion, long range 
transport, climate change

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 17
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
17
• 1960s: Social change and significant national 
environmental movements
– Sierra Club, Wilderness Society
– 1962: Rachel Carson’s ‘Silent Spring’ 
• 1963: Clean Air Act (CAA)
– Broadened federal role in air quality management
• Grants for program development/improvement of state and local air 
pollution control
• Research, training, and technical assistance
• Federal enforcement authority for interstate air pollution problems
• Federal research responsibility for automobile and SOx pollution
• Authority to compile and publish criteria for pollutants

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 18
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
18
• 1965: Motor Vehicle Air Pollution Control Act
– Amendment to 1963 CAA
– Established the National Air Pollution Control 
Administration (NAPCA)
– Authorized DHEW/NAPCA to promulgate motor 
vehicle emissions standards

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 19
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
19
• 1967: Air Quality Act (Amendment to CAA)
– Institution of a regional approach to air pollution 
control and standard setting
– Air Quality Control Regions (AQCR)
– NAPCA to develop/issue air quality criteria and 
control technique info
– States to develop state air quality standards, state 
implementation plan (SIP)

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 20
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
20
 1970: USEPA established (NAPCA eliminated)
• 1970: Clean Air Act Amendments
– Provided for federal enforcement authority
– Stringent auto emissions and fuel standards
– National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS)
• Six Criteria Air Pollutants (CAP)
– New Source Performance Standard (NSPS)
– National Emissions Standards for Hazardous
     Air Pollutants (NESHAPS)
First earth day, 1970

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 21
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
21
• 1977: Clean Air Act Amendments
– Required review of NAAQS every 5 years
– Non-compliance penalties
– New Source Review (NSR) for major sources
– Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD)
– Grant USEPA authority to regulate ozone destroying 
chemicals
• 1977: National Atmospheric Deposition Program 
(NADP) established
– Monitoring trends of acidity in precipitation

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 22
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
22
• 1978: US ban manufacture and sale of CFCs for 
spray cans
• 1980: Acid Precipitation Act
– National Acid Precipitation Assessment Program 
(NAPA)
– Enlarged NADP to National Trends Network (NTN)
• 1980: Election of Ronald Reagan
– “Onslaught” on environmental regulations

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 23
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
23
• 1990: Clean Air Act Amendments
– Reauthorization and update of CAA
– Strengthen measures for attaining air quality standards
– Boundaries of non-attainment areas to include all areas in 
metropolitan area
– Expanded regulation of HAPs
• Max achievable control technology (MACT)
• Establish program for prevention of accidental releases 
– Updated authority and specific requirements for stratospheric 
ozone depletion
– Expanded enforcement powers and penalties
– Criminal sanctions for negligent violations

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 24
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
24
• 2005: Clean Air Interstate Rule (CAIR)
– Cap and trade for O3 and PM
– Replaced by Cross-State Air Pollution Rule (CSAPR) in 2011
• 2007: Supreme court ruling providing EPA authority over 
CO2
• 2015: Volkswagen emissions scandal ($2.8B fine)
• 2015: Clean Power Plan: reduce carbon emissions from 
power plants
• 2016: 1st Trump presidency
– Many environmental policy changes followed

• 6 Criteria Air Pollutants (CAPs):

heading: Particulate Matter (PM) / • A.K.A. aerosol, can be a solid/liquid/mixed
text:
Particulate Matter (PM)
• A.K.A. aerosol, can be a solid/liquid/mixed
• PM10 & PM2.5
– PMs with aerodynamic diameter < 10 or 2.5 µm
• 1 µm =  1x10-6 m
– Can lodge in airway once inhaled. 
– PM2.5 penetrate deep into lungs (alveoli region)
• Many emission sources
– Fire, dust, agriculture, fuel combustion, cars etc…
– Both primary/secondary, natural/man-made sources
• Secondary organic aerosol (SOA) is a major research topic

heading: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2) / • Usually NO and NO2 are measured together
text:
Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2)
• Usually NO and NO2 are measured together
– NO eventually oxidized to NO2
– NO + NO2 = NOx (different from NOy and NOz!)
• NOz = a combination of several reactive nitrogen species
• NOy = NOx + NOz
• Mostly man-made, primary emissions (fuel 
combustion at high temperatures)
– Mobile source, power plants dominates
• Some natural sources
– Lighting generate NOx
– Some plants also emit NOx 33

heading: Ground-level ozone (O3) / • One major component of photochemical smog
text:
Ground-level ozone (O3)
• One major component of photochemical smog
• Ground-level O3 BAD; stratospheric O3 GOOD.
– Health effect when exposed near ground
– Stratospheric O3 layer absorbs harmful UV
• Secondary pollutants, negligible direct emissions 
– Primarily from NOX and VOC, mixing with sunlight
– VOC: Volatile Organic Compounds
• From evaporation of organic solvents, incomplete combustion etc…
• Trees emits VOC (biogenic): mostly isoprene
• Globally, trees emits more VOC than man-made sources
• Ronald Reagan (1981): Trees cause more pollution than 
automobiles do
34

heading: Sulfur Dioxide (SO2) / • From combustion of sulfur-containing fuel
text:
Sulfur Dioxide (SO2)
• From combustion of sulfur-containing fuel
• Primary, anthropogenic sources dominate
– Coal fire power plants is the biggest source
– Also industry, mobile, fire (wild + prescribed)
– Some natural source: sulfur springs
• Major contributor to acid rain, especially 
northeastern US
35

heading: Carbon Monoxide (CO) / • Colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas
text:
Carbon Monoxide (CO)
• Colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas
• Mostly primary, from incomplete fuel combustion
– Mobile source, fire are the biggest ones
• Some plants emits CO (biogenic)
• CO binds with hemoglobin, reduce oxygen 
carrying capacity of blood
36

Lead (Pb)

• Combustion of fuels with lead additives
• Leaded gas phased out → lead in ambient air 
decreased by 99%
– Leaded gas invented by Thomas Midgley Jr. who also 
brought us Freon (CFC)
• Lead particularly toxic to children
• Houses built before 1978 has lead paint

• Chlorofluorocarbons (CFC)
– Contains chlorine (Cl) and fluorine (F)
– Produced synthetically
– Cheap, nontoxic, nonflammable, nonexplosive, 
insoluble, relatively inert
– Used in refrigeration, spray cans, blowing agent
– Average lifetime ~ 75 years
• There are also other halogenated species: 
HCFCs, HFCs, bromine containing chemicals…

heading: Stratospheric ozone chemistry - CFCs / 47
text:
Stratospheric ozone chemistry - CFCs
47
• In stratosphere, CFC break down when exposed 
to far-UV, release ClOx and atomic chlorine
• CFC don’t break down in troposphere (why?)
– Hence climb to stratosphere
• Destruct ozone through the generalized catalytic 
ozone destruction mechanism
Cl + O3 → ClO + O2
ClO + O → Cl + O2
NET:        O + O₃ → 2O₂
active chlorine

heading: Stratospheric ozone chemistry - CFCs / 48
text:
Stratospheric ozone chemistry - CFCs
48
• -Cl chain length: 10 -1,000 (Jacobson, 2002)
– One Cl molecule on average destructs 10-1,000 
ozone molecules in lower and upper stratosphere, 
respectively. Aka chain length
– Bigger chain length number, more powerful ozone 
destruction
• -Br chain length: 100 - 10,000 (Jacobson, 2002)
– Slower reaction, more efficient
• The estimated numbers vary

heading: Stratospheric ozone chemistry - CFCs / 49
text:
Stratospheric ozone chemistry - CFCs
49
• Sink of active chlorine (Cl, ClO)
– Reactions to form reservoir species: HCl and ClONO2
• Hydrochloric acid and chlorine nitrate
– Temporarily store chlorine
– When sunlight present, can photolyzed back to free 
chlorine, continue ozone destruction
• Bromine chemistry is similar

heading: Ozone depletion issues / 50
text:
Ozone depletion issues
50
• Ozone reduction near N/S poles generally 
observed in/near spring time
– Spring time differs for north/south hemisphere
• One factor: Cl and Br in stratosphere & their 
chemistry in polar stratospheric clouds (PSC)
– Recall that active chlorine (Cl, ClO)/Br destroy ozone 
through generalized catalytic mechanism

heading: Ozone depletion process / 53
text:
Ozone depletion process
53
• During polar night (before spring)
– Polar stratospheric clouds (PSC) forms → reactions 
occur inside PSC → convert inactive Cl/Br (such as 
reservoir species HCl and ClONO2) to species that 
are photo-chemically active (Cl2, HOCl, ClNO2 etc)
– Chlorine activation
• Beginning of polar day (early spring)
– Photo-chemically active species go through 
photolysis reaction → release active Cl/Br (Cl, ClO) → 
catalytically destroy ozone

54

heading: Ozone depletion process / 55
text:
Ozone depletion process
55
• Why ozone depletion is less severe in north 
pole?
• Temperature higher in Arctic
– Less PSC formation, less chlorine activation
– Higher temperature due to difference in land cover
• Ocean in Arctic vs land in Antarctic
• Polar vortex not as strong in arctic due to rough terrain

heading: Clean Air Act (CAA) / 4
text:
Clean Air Act (CAA)
4
• First established in 1963, amended multiple times
• Primary & secondary standards:
– Primary: for the protection of human health
– Secondary: for the protection of public welfare
• National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS)
– Regulate six Criteria Air Pollutants (CAPs)

The iterative nature of air quality management
https://www.nap.edu/catalog/10728/air-quality-management-in-the-united-states

heading: Introduction / 6
text:
Introduction
6
• Air quality is a public good 
– Shared resource, value distributed over population
• Air pollutant emissions result from many 
activities that are beneficial to quality of life
– It is not possible or desirable to remove all emissions
• Costs and benefits are often unequally 
distributed

heading: Introduction / 7
text:
Introduction
7
• External cost are often external to the market
– Environmental damage, health impact etc.
– Difficult to calculate accurately 
– Difficult to attribute in a meaningful way to individual 
purchaser
• The Tragedy of the Commons
• Regulations are “unproductive resources” 
• Much work on trying to figure out how to provide 
incentives that work with/not against market

heading: Non-Regulatory Legal Remedies / 8
text:
Non-Regulatory Legal Remedies
8
• Tort Law
– Individuals file civil suit against source to recover damage or to 
abate the problem
– Nuisance and trespass principles used to air pollution 
historically
• Nuisance
– Act resulting in “unreasonable” interference with use and 
enjoyment of one’s property
• Trespass 
– Physical violation of land owners right to exclusive possession 
– Used for smoke historically

heading: Regulatory Air Quality Management / Strategies
text:
Regulatory Air Quality Management 
Strategies
9
• All regulatory and policy measures implemented 
in an attempt to control concentrations and 
effects of air pollutants
• Usually refers to control by some political entity
– HC EPC, FL DEP, US EPA, US OSHA, US FDA etc…
• Types of management strategies: 
– Air quality standards, emissions standards, 
economics-based approaches

heading: Ambient Air Quality Standards / 10
text:
Ambient Air Quality Standards
10
• Levels of pollutant concentrations in air that are 
allowable/acceptable
– Generally set at a level considered not harmful
– Based on principle of threshold levels
– Not necessarily appropriate for all pollutants
– Provide “margin of safety” for sensitive populations
– Lower than occupational values set for healthy adults

heading: Ambient Air Quality Standards / 11
text:
Ambient Air Quality Standards
11
• Issues with ambient air quality standards
– Require air quality monitoring to determine levels
– Local exposures not adequately represented
– Doesn’t deal with how to achieve these levels
– Control and management practices must be 
implemented to achieve standards
• This is generally fairly complicated undertaking

heading: Emissions Standards / 12
text:
Emissions Standards
12
• Levels of acceptable emissions
• Based often on technological achievability and 
economic costs
• Simpler to manage
• Problematic because not necessarily related to 
actual air quality

heading: Economics-Based Approaches / 13
text:
Economics-Based Approaches
13
• Provide a system that provides incentives 
for decreasing pollution
• Include cost-benefit analysis and market-
based policies

heading: Cost-Benefit Analyses / 14
text:
Cost-Benefit Analyses
14
• Attempt to determine the appropriate level of 
pollution
• Industry groups are very interested in having 
cost-benefit analyses performed
• Problems
– Difficult to quantify all external costs
• Loss of sense of community, changes in ecosystems etc.. 
– Very difficult to deal with equity

heading: Market-based policies / 15
text:
Market-based policies
15
 Market-based policies involves the bubble concept, 
emission trading and allowance
 Bubble concept
 Existing plants or groups of plants are considered one entity from 
emissions point of view
 Facilities have flexibility to increase emissions of one process if 
overall emissions are the same or lower.
 Flexibility can lead to most cost effective reduction strategies 
without unreasonably hampering process innovation

heading: Market-based policies / 16
text:
Market-based policies
16
• Facility is given an “emission allowance”
• Excess emission reduction → Emissions 
reduction credits
– The credits may be sold are traded to other facilities
• Apply economic value to emissions reductions
• Effective method

heading: Pollution charges / 17
text:
Pollution charges
17
• Less used method
• Charges by amount of emissions
• Difficult to set appropriate charges 
• Must be enough to stimulate reductions without 
being unreasonably burdensome

heading: National Ambient Air Quality Standards / (NAAQS)
text:
National Ambient Air Quality Standards 
(NAAQS)
20
• 1970 CAA authorized EPA to establish NAAQS. 
• Primary & secondary standards:
– Primary: for the protection of human health
– Secondary: for the protection of public welfare
• Six Criteria Air Pollutants (CAPs):
– O3, CO, NO2, SO2, Pb, PM (PM2.5 & PM10)
• Air Quality Criteria documents present scientific 
evidence linking pollutant so health and welfare effects 
(for establishing the appropriate standards)

State Implementation Plans (SIPs)
21
• States required to develop and submit plans for the 
implementation, enforcement and maintenance of 
NAAQS 
• Plans include
– Legal authority for regulation and compliance
– Emissions limitations and control requirements
– Permitting
– Monitoring, modeling, 
– Data collection and analysis
– Episode Control Plans:  
• Provisions for an air pollution episode or emergency
Region 4 SIPs: https://www.epa.gov/air-quality-implementation-plans/approved-air-
quality-implementation-plans-region-4

heading: Non Attainment Areas / 22
text:
Non Attainment Areas 
22
• Areas not in attainment of NAAQS are designated as 
Non-attainment Areas
• Significant because does not allow new sources 
(theoretically), since dangerous to health already
• Concerns with limits on economic growth in non-
attainment areas have led to
– Emissions offset policy (no net increase from a facility)
– Alternative of Lowest Achievable Emission Rate for new sources
– Postponement of deadlines for attainment

Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD)

pollutants) into:

NAAQS)

areas, national monuments, national parks (> about

emissions standards

categories and pollutants

New source rules

• New Source Review (NSR)

heading: Operating Permits / 31
text:
Operating Permits 
31
• All existing major stationary sources must have a permit 
• Recording in one document all air pollutions 
requirements 
• Permits contain 
– enforceable emission limits
– monitoring and reporting requirements
– compliance plan with an enforceable schedule
• Burden of proof for compliance is on the emission source
• Permit fees to pay for regulatory programs
• Review and renewal every 5 years

State or Local Air Monitoring Stations

4
• Biggest network

• Primary purpose: comparison to NAAQS
– Must use Federal reference method (FRM), Federal equivalent method 
(FEM), or Approved Regional Method (ARM) monitors 
• Additional purposes may also include:
– Provide air pollution data to the general public in a timely manner
– Support compliance with air quality standards and emissions strategy 
development
– Support air pollution research studies
• SLAMS network include NCore, PAMS, and CSN networks

heading: SLAMS location considerations / 5

National Core (NCore) 
6
• Part of SLAMS network
• Characterize regional and urban patterns of air pollution
• Comprehensive multi-pollutant measurement
– PM2.5, speciated PM2.5, PM10-2.5, speciated PM10-2.5, O3, 
SO2, CO, NO/NO2/NOy, basic meteorology
• Monitors for all gases (except for O3) needs to be more 
sensitive than standard FRM/FEM monitors
– Likely some pollutant concentrations are low

Stations (PAMS)

strategies for ozone control
• Monitor ozone, NOx, and VOC to obtain more 
comprehensive and representative data on ozone air 
pollution

some co-located with PAMS network
• A subset called Speciation Trends Network (STN) 
provide long-term chemical trend of PM composition
– Annual and seasonal spatial characterization of aerosols
– Air quality trends and control progress tracking
– Compare speciation data with IMPROVE network data
– Develop emission control strategies

progress toward emission and risk reduction goals

near monitors
• Provide quality assured air toxic data for risk 
characterization

activities

model performance

mandatory class I areas

visibility-protected class I areas where practical

heading: Ideal aerosol sampling system / • Excludes precipitation from the sampled aerosol
text:
Ideal aerosol sampling system
• Excludes precipitation from the sampled aerosol
• Provides a representative ambient aerosol 
sample with minimal diffusional and inertial 
losses
• Provides aerosol particles at a low relative 
humidity (< 40%)
• Minimizes the evaporation of volatile particulate 
species
15

heading: Inlet design considerations / • Sample air should be brought into the laboratory through a vertical
text:
Inlet design considerations
• Sample air should be brought into the laboratory through a vertical 
stack.
• Inlet that is high enough above ground level to minimize local 
influences (a minimum height of 2 m above the roof, even higher 
inlets may be required for obstructed sites).
• If possible, the sampling duct should be brought through the roof of 
the laboratory. If this is not possible, then a gradual bend in the inlet 
pipe is acceptable.
• High aerosol transmission efficiency that does not vary with wind 
direction or wind speed. This can be achieved with a vertical air duct 
with a cover that excludes drizzle, rain and snow mounted on top of 
the inlet duct.
• The inlet should have a particle cut-off diameter corresponding to 
sampling goal under ambient conditions.
16

heading: Tubing and flow splitters / • For the sampling of particles, the pipes should be made of conductive
text:
Tubing and flow splitters
• For the sampling of particles, the pipes should be made of conductive 
material, and electrically grounded.
• Short pieces of tubing might be replaced by conductive silicone tubing, 
which is elastic and conducting at the same time.
• A perfect inlet installation also avoids sources of turbulence (bends, 
connectors) as best as possible (turbulence enhances particle losses 
due to diffusion) and keeps the sampling lines as short as possible.
• Isokinetic flow splitter: a sample is removed from the core of the main 
aerosol flow rather than from streamlines near the wall of the main 
pipe. This ensures a representative sampling especially of coarse and 
nano-particles.
17

heading: Sample drying / • Dry sampling maintains the RH at a sufficiently low
text:
Sample drying
• Dry sampling maintains the RH at a sufficiently low 
range that hygroscopic growth effects are minimized.
• The preferred methods for reducing the relative humidity 
are to remove water vapor with a diffusion or membrane 
dryer, alternatively to reduce the dewpoint temperature 
by diluting the sample with filtered, dry air.
• An alternative method is to reduce the RH to 40% by 
modest heating to a temperature not to exceed 40°C (to 
minimize loss of semi-volatile species).

stressed, electrical charges of opposite polarity appear

direction depending upon the polarity of the field.

crystalline quartz with a certain frequency

TEOM versions
• Differential Tapered-Element Oscillating Microbalance
– A size-selective inlet followed by a diffusion dryer, an ESP, and the TEOM 
mass sensor operated at reduced filter temperature (e.g., 30°C).
– The ESP is alternately switched on and off (for equal time periods, e.g., 5

adsorption of gas species.
• TEOM Equipped with a Filter Dynamics Measurement System
– A cold filter maintained at 4°C instead of an electrostatic precipitator to 
remove particles.
– Alternate every 6 min between ambient air sampling (base flow) and purging 
the sample filter with particle-free air (reference flow).

heading: Other detection methods / 6

Other detection methods

• Chemiluminescence
– Chemical reaction used to excite molecules which then 
luminescence (give off light)
– Degree of luminescence gives concentration

• UV Fluorescence
– Similar to photometry but light given off (at a specific 
wavelength) due to excitation of molecule by UV light

heading: Ambient Air Quality Standards / 9
text:
Ambient Air Quality Standards
9
• Regulatory monitoring
– Use Federal Reference Method (FRM) and Federal Equivalent 
Method (FEM) instrument
• Accurate but costly: equipment, power, site, maintenance, data 
transmission, personal etc
– Measurement stations limited spatially and temporally
• Pollution concentration could change drastically spatially 
and temporally
– More so for primary pollutants, especially traffic-related 
pollutants such as CO, NOx 
FL monitoring network in FL: https://floridadep.gov/air/air-monitoring/content/air-quality-today
Oakland, CA Google Street View vehicle monitoring: 
https://www.edf.org/airqualitymaps/oakland/pollution-and-health-concerns-west-oakland

heading: Low(er)-cost air quality monitor / • Uses lower-cost sensor to measure pollution
text:
Low(er)-cost air quality monitor
• Uses lower-cost sensor to measure pollution

– Mostly optical particle counters
– Count particle # at limited sizes, convert to mass
• For gases pollutants
– A wide variety of sensors
– Metal oxides, electrochemical, photochemical, non-
dispersive infrared etc
• Able to measure near-real-time concentration
• Easy integration into “smart” networks

heading: Summary / • Smart and connected air quality sensor devices has
text:
Summary
• Smart and connected air quality sensor devices has 
great potentials to substantially change the landscape of 
traditional air quality monitoring
• Currently a booming and fast-expanding market, with 
many devices with varying performances
• Data quality remain a significant concern
• Without careful QA/QC, data collected could be 
misleading, or even useless
• The vast majority of smart air sensor data can NOT be 
used for regulatory decision making

Gas Scattering

 Gas Scattering

heading: Gas Absorption / 23
text:
Gas Absorption
23
 Gas Absorption
 Only a few gases absorb visible wavelength
 NO2 (< 0.71 µm)
◼ Most important gas absorber, especially in polluted air
 NO3 (< 0.67 µm)
◼ Quickly go away with presence of sunlight
◼ Not very important to visibility

◼ Not very important to visibility since relatively weak absorber 
for visible light

heading: Particle Scattering / 28
text:
Particle Scattering
28
• Real index of refraction varies for different 
wavelengths of light
• Particle in different size ranges scatter differently
– Smaller than wavelength (D/λ < 0.03): Raleigh 
scattering (forward and backward). Generally, for 
particles < 0.05 µm
– Same order as wavelength, 0.03 < D/λ < 32: Mie 
scattering (preferentially forward)
– More forward as particle size increases
– Generally particle > 100 µm geometric scattering

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 7
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
7
• 1960s: Social change and significant national 
environmental movements
– Sierra Club, Wilderness Society
– 1962: Rachel Carson’s ‘Silent Spring’ 
• 1963: Clean Air Act (CAA)
– Broadened federal role in air quality management
• Grants for program development/improvement of state and local air 
pollution control
• Research, training, and technical assistance
• Federal enforcement authority for interstate air pollution problems
• Federal research responsibility for automobile and SOx pollution
• Authority to compile and publish criteria for pollutants

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 8
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
8
• 1965: Motor Vehicle Air Pollution Control Act
– Amendment to 1963 CAA
– Established the National Air Pollution Control 
Administration (NAPCA)
– Authorized DHEW/NAPCA to promulgate motor 
vehicle emissions standards

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 9
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
9
• 1967: Air Quality Act (Amendment to CAA)
– Institution of a regional approach to air pollution 
control and standard setting
– Air Quality Control Regions (AQCR)
– NAPCA to develop/issue air quality criteria and 
control technique info
– States to develop state air quality standards, state 
implementation plan (SIP)

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 10
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
10
 1970: USEPA established (NAPCA eliminated)
• 1970: Clean Air Act Amendments
– Provided for federal enforcement authority
– Stringent auto emissions and fuel standards
– National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS)
• Six Criteria Air Pollutants (CAP)
– New Source Performance Standard (NSPS)
– National Emissions Standards for Hazardous
Air Pollutants (NESHAPS)
First earth day, 1970

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 11
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
11
• 1977: Clean Air Act Amendments
– Required review of NAAQS every 5 years
– Non-compliance penalties
– Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD)
– New Source Review (NSR) for major sources
– Grant USEPA authority to regulate ozone destroying 
chemicals
• 1977: National Atmospheric Deposition Program 
(NADP) established
– Monitoring trends of acidity in precipitation

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 12
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
12
• 1978: US ban manufacture and sale of CFCs for 
spray cans
• 1980: Acid Precipitation Act
– National Acid Precipitation Assessment Program 
(NAPA)
– Enlarged NADP to National Trends Network (NTN)
• 1980: Election of Ronald Reagan
– “Onslaught” on environmental regulations

heading: Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History / 13
text:
Brief U.S. Federal Legislative History 
13
• 1990: Clean Air Act Amendments
– Reauthorization and update of CAA
– Strengthen measures for attaining air quality standards
– Boundaries of non-attainment areas to include all areas in 
metropolitan area
– Expanded regulation of HAPs
• Max achievable control technology (MACT)
• Establish program for prevention of accidental releases 
– Updated authority and specific requirements for stratospheric 
ozone depletion
– Expanded enforcement powers and penalties
– Criminal sanctions for negligent violations

text:

• 2005: Clean Air Interstate Rule (CAIR)
– Cap and trade for O3 and PM
– Replaced by Cross-State Air Pollution Rule (CSAPR) in 2011
• 2007: Supreme court ruling providing EPA authority over 
CO2
• 2015: Volkswagen emissions scandal ($2.8B fine)
• 2015: Clean Power Plan: reduce carbon emissions from 
power plants
• 2016: Mr. Donald Trump elected POTUS
– Many environmental policy changes followed

heading: CAPs & HAPs / • 6 Criteria Air Pollutants (CAPs):
text:
CAPs & HAPs
• 6 Criteria Air Pollutants (CAPs):
– O3, CO, NO2, SO2, Pb, PM (PM2.5 & PM10)
– Concentration level set in NAAQS (in CAA)
– Ubiquitous, most harmful to health and environment
• 187 Hazardous Air Pollutants (HAPs)
– A.K.A. toxic air pollutants or air toxics
– Known/suspected to cause cancer, or other serious 
health or environmental effects
– Goal: reduce emissions (NESHAPS)
– Primary, man-made emissions dominates
20

heading: Particulate Matter (PM) / • A.K.A. aerosol, can be a solid/liquid/mixed
text:
Particulate Matter (PM)
• A.K.A. aerosol, can be a solid/liquid/mixed
• PM10 & PM2.5
– PMs with aerodynamic diameter < 10 or 2.5 µm
• 1 µm =  1x10-6 m
– Can lodge in airway once inhaled. 
– PM2.5 penetrate deep into lungs (alveoli region)
• Many emission sources
– Fire, dust, agriculture, fuel combustion, cars etc…
– Both primary/secondary, natural/man-made sources
• Secondary organic aerosol (SOA) is a major research topic
21

heading: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2) / • Usually NO and NO2 are measured together
text:
Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2)
• Usually NO and NO2 are measured together
– NO eventually oxidized to NO2
– NO + NO2 = NOx (different from NOy and NOz!)
• Mostly man-made, primary emissions (fuel 
combustion at high temperatures)
– Mobile source, power plants dominates
• Some natural sources
– Lighting generate NOx
– Some plants also emit NOx
22

heading: Ground-level ozone (O3) / • One major component of photochemical smog
text:
Ground-level ozone (O3)
• One major component of photochemical smog
• Ground-level O3 BAD; stratospheric O3 GOOD.
– Health effect when exposed near ground
– Stratospheric O3 layer absorbs harmful UV
• Secondary pollutants, negligible direct emissions 
– Primarily from NOX and VOC, mixing with sunlight
– VOC: Volatile Organic Compounds
• From evaporation of organic solvents, incomplete combustion etc…
• Trees emits VOC (biogenic): mostly isoprene
• Globally, trees emits more VOC than man-made sources
• Ronald Reagan (1981): Trees cause more pollution than 
automobiles do
23

heading: Sulfur Dioxide (SO2) / • From combustion of sulfur-containing fuel
text:
Sulfur Dioxide (SO2)
• From combustion of sulfur-containing fuel
• Primary, anthropogenic sources dominate
– Coal fire power plants is the biggest source
– Also industry, mobile, fire (wild + prescribed)
– Some natural source: sulfur springs
• Major contributor to acid rain, especially 
northeastern US
24

heading: Carbon Monoxide (CO) / • Colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas
text:
Carbon Monoxide (CO)
• Colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas
• Mostly primary, from incomplete fuel combustion
– Mobile source, fire are the biggest ones
• Some plants emits CO (biogenic)
• CO binds with hemoglobin, reduce oxygen 
carrying capacity of blood
• Don’t BBQ indoor
25

heading: Lead (Pb) / • Particulate lead
text:
Lead (Pb)
• Particulate lead
• Combustion of fuels with lead additives
• Leaded gas phased out → lead in ambient air 
decreased by 99%
– Leaded gas invented by Thomas Midgley Jr. who also 
brought us Freon (CFC)
• Lead particularly toxic to children
• Houses built before 1978 has lead paint
26

heading: Understanding Stability: / Vertical air motion
text:
Understanding Stability: 
Vertical air motion
11
• Buoyancy
– Air hotter than surrounding is less dense (and rises)
• Rising and falling air leads to 
– vertical overturning and mixing
– pollutant dispersal/dilution due to turbulence
• Atmosphere can enhance or suppress this
– Stable – atmosphere resists vertical motion
– Unstable – atmosphere enhances vertical motion
– Neutral – atmosphere does neither

– Empirically derived based on observational data
– Proposed for hot, bend-over plumes, less accurate for cold and 
wet plumes (e.g. those coming out of wet scrubber)
– Here we discuss them in unstable and stable conditions

heading: Max ground concentrations / • Max ground concentration does not always
text:
Max ground concentrations
• Max ground concentration does not always 
occur at minimum wind speed
– Yes, C inversely associated with u
– But, plume rise is also inversely associated with u
• The wind speed that results in max ground 
concentration is called critical wind speed

heading: Downwash
text: Downwash

heading: Downwash / • As wind blows past blunt objects, flow
text:
Downwash
• As wind blows past blunt objects, flow 
disturbances occur, and low pressure zones are 
created.  Depending on wind speed, vortexes 
and eddies are formed. These eddies can trap 
stack releases and bring them quickly to the 
ground. 
Example 1: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o3wPbPgQBhA
Example 2: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OqRUtRytanI

heading: Downwash / • Most dispersion models has taken account the effect of
text:
Downwash
• Most dispersion models has taken account the effect of 
downwash
• Many models, such as AERMOD, uses PRIME (plume 
rise model enhancements). More information see 
Schulman et al 2000
– https://doi.org/10.1080/10473289.2000.10464017
• Ways to reduce downwash:
– Increase exit velocity  smaller diameter
• 1.5 times expected maximum stack tip velocity
– Engineering method, turning wind

Topics
• Overview of air quality models

heading: To start with….. / 3
text:
To start with…..
3
• What is a model?
– A representation of a system
• To investigate its properties and/or perform predictions
– Vary substantially in complexity
• Why we need model in air quality field?
– Measurements are expensive
– Measurements are limited, spatially and temporally
– Need to answer “what if” questions

heading: To start with….. / 4
text:
To start with…..
4
• “all models are wrong”, but useful
• There are always errors and biases in 
model outputs
• Caution must be taken to evaluate model 
outputs, and to identify and correct biases 
and errors

heading: To start with….. / • Mean to, mechanistically, mathematically
text:
To start with…..
• Mean to, mechanistically, mathematically 
approximate actual physical chemical process in 
the atmosphere
– Not a strict definition
• Use model to investigate the fate and transport 
of chemical species in the atmosphere
– Note that this is for air quality purposes
– Many advanced models include more than just 
atmosphere, and are capable of more purposes

heading: Types of air quality models / • Spatial scale
text:
Types of air quality models
• Spatial scale
– Micro (hundreds of meters), urban (hundreds of km), regional 
(thousands of km), continental (several thousands of km), global
• Temporal scale
– Short-term (up to dozens of days), long-term (years)
• Characterization of transport
– Eulerian vs Lagrangian
• Dimensions
– Zero (box model), 1D (column), 2D, 3D
• Target problems
– Photochemical, acid deposition, aerosol, source apportionment, street 
canyon etc
• Mechanism
– Dispersion, Chemical Transport Model (CTM), Computational Fluid 
Dynamics (CFD) etc

heading: Lagrangian vs Eulerian approach / 7
text:
Lagrangian vs Eulerian approach
7
• Lagrangian: Focus on one ‘piece’ of pollutant, track it 
through space and time (stalker)

heading: Lagrangian vs Eulerian approach / 8
text:
Lagrangian vs Eulerian approach
8
• Eulerian: Focus on the same area, estimate spatial 
concentrations distributions at each time step (snapshot)
https://www.sron.nl/atmospheric-modelling

Box model

0-D models

heading: Gaussian dispersion models / • Steady-state vs non-steady-state models
text:
Gaussian dispersion models
• Steady-state vs non-steady-state models
• Steady-state
– Assume homogeneous meteorological fields
– Usually no “memory” effects
• Non-steady-state
– Spatially varying meteorological fields
– “Remembers” concentration from previous time-step 
(usually hour)

17
• Pollutant modeled as “puff” or “particles”
• Movements of “puff” or “particles” are tracked 
spatially and temporally at each time step
– Normally using 3-D meteorological field data from 
weather forecasting models
• Mainly applied in urban scale
– Can be applied for regional scale
• Long range transportation
• Examples: CALPUFF,

heading: Eulerian chemical transport models / 19
text:
Eulerian chemical transport models
19
• Discretize the study area into grid cells
• Do not try to solve for meteorological fields
– Data from weather forecasting models (e.g. WRF)
• At each time step
– Solve for pollutant concentrations in each cell 
altogether from groups of mass balance equations
– Homogeneous concentration distribution within cell
• Example: CMAQ, CAMx, UCD
• Generally applied in large scale, from regional 
scale (e.g. Eastern US) to global

heading: Computational fluid dynamics models / 20
text:
Computational fluid dynamics models
20
• Virtually all use Eulerian approach
• Solve for meteorological field and concentrations 
at the same time
• Generally applied from continental to global 
scale
• Examples: GEOS-CHEM, WRF-CHEM, WRF-
CMAQ etc

secondary and radical species
• Or you can choose to simplify things by lumping 
(aggregating) chemicals together

research center); RADM2 (2nd Regional acid deposition model 
mechanism); MPRM (Morphecule photochemical reaction 
mechanism)

heading: The NEI / • USEPA maintains the National Emissions Inventory
text:
The NEI
• USEPA maintains the National Emissions Inventory 
(NEI), a “comprehensive and detailed estimate of air 
emissions of criteria pollutants, criteria precursors, and 
hazardous air pollutants”
– Home: https://www.epa.gov/air-emissions-inventories

heading: The NEI / • NEI data collected/estimated using both top-
text:
The NEI
• NEI data collected/estimated using both top-
down and bottom-up methods
– Top-down: estimate total emission in an area
• E.g: emissions from dry cleaning facilities in Orange County
• E = A X EF: Emission = Activity X Emission Factor
• Available for the area of focus for an entire time (a county in a year)
– Bottom-up: estimate/collect emission amount at 
individual source
• E.g: Continuous Emission Monitoring System (CEMS) data at 
stacks
• Can at specific location and very detailed

heading: SMOKE / • SMOKE (Sparse Matrix Operator Kerner Emissions) is a
text:
SMOKE
• SMOKE (Sparse Matrix Operator Kerner Emissions) is a 
widely used emission model in the US
– Home: https://www.cmascenter.org/smoke/
• Prepare emission data for air quality models
– Inputs in the US includes NEI
– Also do speciation for different chemistry mechanisms
• Types of emission handled by SMOKE
– Point, non-point (area), biogenic, mobile, others
• When only total emission is known
– Spatial surrogate: used to spatially allocate emission
– Temporal profile: used to temporally allocation emission

• Area: Spatial and temporal allocation
• Mobile: MOVES (Motor Vehicle Emission Simulator)
– We will learn more later in this class
• Biogenic: BEIS (Biogenic Emission Inventory System) or 
MEGAN (Model of Emissions of Gases and Aerosols 
from Nature)

• CAL3QHC reads a control file, which provides all 
data/information needed for modeling
• CAL3QHC uses three formats to read control file
– Character: text string, need to be single quoted
• E.g: ‘this is a test link 1 2 3’
– Integer: number with no decimal points
– Real: number with decimal points

heading: Control file: Line 1 / Name Type Description

Name Type Description
JOB Character Job title, < 40 character
ATIM Real Averaging time (min). 60 in most case
ZO Real Surface roughness length (cm)
VS Real
Settling velocity (cm/s). How fast particle is settling. 
Usually 0
VD Real
Deposition velocity (cm/s). “Equivalent” velocity for dry 
and wet deposition. Usually 0
NR Integer # receptor, max = 60
SCAL Real
Scaling factor to convert input number to meter. 1 if inputs 
are in meter. 0.3048 if inputs are in feet
IOPT Integer 1 output feet; 0 output meter
IDEBUG Integer 1 for more detailed diagnostic information. 0 disable

heading: Queue link / • Link length: only used to determine direction for queue

• Link length: only used to determine direction for queue

• Signal type
– 1: pretimed: fixed signal time length
– 2: actuated: all signals triggered as needed
• E.g.: loop-detector or push-button
– 3: semi-actuated. 
• Some signal triggered as needed, some not
• Arrival rate
– Traffic signal time is designed to optimize traffic flow
– Best case: drive through several intersections without stop
– Worst case: run into every red light at every intersection

– 1 = Worst: cars lined up at beginning of red
– 2 = Below ave: cars lined up in middle of red
– 3 = Average: random arrivals
– 4 = Above ave: dense cars arrives during green
– 5 = Best: dense cars at beginning of green

determine the worst case or maximum concentrations 
that might occur
• Do screening is to eliminate the need to run a refined, 
and more costly, air quality model and analysis
• “AERSCREEN View” is a graphical interface to 
AERSCREEN developed by Lake Environment
– AERSCREEN is open source and free. “AERSCREEN View” is 
not

heading: AERSCREEN / • Based on only a few inputs, AERSCREEN
text:
AERSCREEN
• Based on only a few inputs, AERSCREEN 
automatically configures and runs AERMOD
– Eliminated much efforts in running a detailed 
AERMOD analysis
• AERSCREEN download webpage:
– https://www.epa.gov/scram/air-quality-dispersion-
modeling-screening-models
– Download these
• AERSCREEN & MAKEMET code and executables
• AERSCREEN user guide
• Testcase & README txt file

heading: AERSCREEN components / • AERSCREEN calls these components when needed
text:
AERSCREEN components
• AERSCREEN calls these components when needed
– MAKEMET: generate a combinations of meteorological 
conditions for AERSCREEN
– AERMOD: the actual dispersion model AERSCREEN is running, 
but with all parameters auto configured based on user inputs
– BPIPPRM: building downwash module, used only when 
downwash is enabled
– AERSURFACE: generate surface characteristics, used only 
when detailed surface characteristics are needed
– AERMAP: generate ground elevation data, used only when 
detailed elevation data are needed
• Only needs to run AERSCREEN
– Input data may need to be prepared for each component

heading: Initial information / • AERSCREEN will attempt to read “aerscreen.inp”, which
text:
Initial information
• AERSCREEN will attempt to read “aerscreen.inp”, which 
was generated during previous runs and contains all 
information needed
– If no such file, then start a new run
• Source type:
– POINT: regular point source (a stack)
– POINTCAP: stack with a rain hat
– POINTHOR: horizontal stack
– FLARE: model flare burning
– VOLUME: volume source (e.g. a cube emitting from all sides)
– AREA: rectangle source (e.g. land fill)
– AREACIRC: Circular area sources

heading: Source information / • Information on emissions from source
text:
Source information
• Information on emissions from source
– Different for different source types
– We will focus on point source only
– Emission Rate (g/s), Stack Height (meters): Stack Diameter 
(meters), Stack Temperature (K)
– Exit Velocity or Flow Rate
• Others
– Rural or urban: affect how vertical wind varies, and surface 
characteristics
– Minimum ambient distance: closest receptor distance downwind 
of source
– NO2 chemistry: only for NO2, calculate ratios of NO and NO2

heading: Building downwash / • Option to use an existing BPIPPRM input file
text:
Building downwash
• Option to use an existing BPIPPRM input file
– Bypass following inputs, details see addendum:
– https://www.epa.gov/scram/air-quality-dispersion-modeling-
related-model-support-programs#bpipprm
• Building height (feet or meters)
• Maximum building horizontal dimension (feet or meters)
• Minimum building horizontal dimension (feet or meters)
• Degrees from North of maximum building horizontal 
dimension (0-179 degrees)
• Degrees from North of stack location relative to building 
center (0-360 degrees)
• Distance between stack and building center (feet or 
meters)

Building downwash

heading: Terrain / • If choose to account for spatial varying terrain variation,
text:
Terrain
• If choose to account for spatial varying terrain variation, 
need to have external terrain elevation data
– Data file name listed in demlist.txt
– We will discuss more when we come to AERMAP
An example of digital elevation map
https://gis.stackexchange.com/questions/68965/precision-vs-resolution-in-elevation-data

heading: Terrain / • Probe distance (meters)
text:
Terrain
• Probe distance (meters)
– Furthest distance to calculate concentration
• Include discrete receptor distances
– Option to include user defined location for conc calc
• Flagpole receptors
– Calculate concentration at higher elevation
• Source elevation, or AERMAP determine source 
elevation from digital terrain data
• Source coordinates (geographic or UTM)
• NAD datum (NAD 27 or 83)
• UTM zone (if UTM coordinates entered)

heading: NAD & UTM / • Used to account for the curvature of earth
text:
NAD & UTM
• Used to account for the curvature of earth
• NAD: North American Datum of 1927/1983
– Datum: coordinate system defines the shape of earth
– NAD 27/83 best suits north American
• UTM: Universal Transverse Mercator coordinate 
system
– A simple algorithm to expand round earth to a flat 
surface, using a datum
– Instead of uneven lat and lon, now you have a evenly 
distributed X and Y

heading: Meteorology data / • Minimum and maximum ambient air temperatures
text:
Meteorology data
• Minimum and maximum ambient air temperatures 
(Fahrenheit or Kelvin)
• Minimum wind speed (m/s)
– Recall dispersion model do not work well under calm condition
• Anemometer height (m)
– 10 m is the standard height
• Surface characteristics
– Can be user-entered single value; AERMET tables or listed in an 
external file (varying by certain time periods)
– We will discuss the time varying option in AERMET

heading: Meteorology data / • Albedo: % of incoming radiation reflected back
text:
Meteorology data
• Albedo: % of incoming radiation reflected back
– 0 for perfect black body, 1 for perfect reflective surface
• Bowen ratio: ratio between sensible heat and latent heat
– Sensible heat: energy used to increase temp
– Latent heat: energy used to change phase, no temp change
– How much energy were used to evaporate water, but not used to 
increase temperature
– < 0.1 for large water body and up to 10 for dry dessert
• Surface roughness length (Z0)
– Lowest height at which wind speed is zero
– Over Z0 wind increases according to a power law
– < 1 mm in very flat surface, a few meter for urban region

heading: Meteorology data / • Surface friction velocity (u*)
text:
Meteorology data
• Surface friction velocity (u*)
– A scaling parameter. a measure of the vertical transport of 
horizontal momentum
– Past studies showed that under low wind speed and stable 
condition, u* need to be modified to get better results
– Optional to adjust u*
• Convective velocity (w*)
– Internally calculated, describes the speed of vertical transport 
due to convection (buoyancy gained from temp difference)
• Monin-Obukhov length (L)
– Internally calculated, one way to describes stability
– L < 0: unstable, L > 0: stable

heading: Meteorology data / • A look up table for Albedo, Bowen ratio and Z0
text:
Meteorology data
• A look up table for Albedo, Bowen ratio and Z0
(from CARB) is provided on webcourse
• AERMOD/AERSCREEN uses two 
meteorological files
– Surface observation and vertical distribution profile
– Default: .sfc and .pfl
– Collected at surface met stations and usually from 
balloon sounding (aka upper air sounding)
• https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9v-aqz18puI

heading: Fumigation / • AERSCREEN can account for two fumigations
text:
Fumigation
• AERSCREEN can account for two fumigations
– Inversion break-up and shoreline
– Inherited from SCREEN3 model
– Only for certain conditions
• Elevated inversion
Shoreline fumigation
https://atmos.washington.edu/~justin/radar_project/clearair.htm
 Inversion break-up fumigation
https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Figure-9-Illustrating-
the-effect-of-inversion-break-up_283653069_fig4

heading: AERMOD / • American Meteorological Society/Environmental
text:
AERMOD
• American Meteorological Society/Environmental 
Protection Agency Regulatory Model 
• EPA recommended/preferred dispersion model 
for near field applications
– Replaced Industrial Source Complex (ISC) in 2006
– ISC has a life-span of > 20 years, very widely used
• Refined model applications
– Recall AERSCREEN is the screening version

heading: Components of AERMOD / • AERMET: meteorological data preprocessor
text:
Components of AERMOD
• AERMET: meteorological data preprocessor
– AERSURFACE: for surface characteristics
– AERMINUTE: for 1-min ASOS data
• AERMAP: terrain data preprocessor
• AERMOD: uses input data (meteorological, 
terrain data etc) to perform refined analysis
– BPIPPRIM: a multi-building dimensions program 
incorporating the GEP technical procedures for 
building downwash applications.

heading: AERMET overview
text: AERMET overview

heading: AERMET / • Process surface and upper air data for use by AERMOD
text:
AERMET
• Process surface and upper air data for use by AERMOD
• Requires:
– Surface characteristics: albedo etc
– Surface meteorological observations 
• Hourly National Weather Services (NWS) observations 
• Automated Surface Observation System (ASOS) data
– Upper air soundings (Radiosondes, Rawinsondes)
• Usually 00:00 and 12:00 GMT; ±1 hour common
• Special soundings may available for other times
– Or, site-specific data for surface
• Data collected by a facility, may not be on-site, no fixed format, 
need to let AERMET know what variables are in there
– Or, data from numerical weather model (such as WRF)
• Require other tools; also commercially available

heading: AERMET / • The major function of AERMET is to
text:
AERMET
• The major function of AERMET is to
– Extract and QA raw, archived observational data
• Upper air, surface, and on-site data
– Calculate required meteorological parameters for 
AERMOD modeling needs
• 1-min ASOS data processed by AERMINUTE were 
combined here (already QA’ed)
• Output to two files: surface and profile

heading: Contents of surface data / • Pressure
text:
Contents of surface data
• Pressure
• Temperatures
• Precipitation (type and intensity) 
• Humidity
• Wind direction, speed and character (gusts etc) 
• Cloud height and quantity
• Visibility, including fog, haze, dust
• More information maybe collected such as start and end

heading: Format of surface data / • ISHD (ISH, ISD) product. Integrated Surface Hourly Data
text:
Format of surface data
• ISHD (ISH, ISD) product. Integrated Surface Hourly Data
– Compilation of global hourly surface observations from > 35,000 
stations worldwide
– TD-3505 format. Reports in GMT time
– Do not use abbreviated ISHD
• ASOS 1-minutes wind data
– Automated sensor collected data. > 900 stations in US
– TD-6405 format. 
– Has to be pre-processed using AERMINUTE

heading: Format of surface data / • AERMET also accepts other, some are really old, formats
text:
Format of surface data
• AERMET also accepts other, some are really old, formats
– CD-144: ended 12/31/95
– SCRAM (1/1/1984 – 12/31/1992)
– SAMSON (1/1/1961 – 12/31/1990)
– HUSWO (1/1/1990 – 12/31/1995)
– TD-3280
• Some of these data only available on CD/DVD and even 
on tapes

heading: Format of upper air data / • Collected from twice a day soundings
text:
Format of upper air data
• Collected from twice a day soundings
– Pressure, temperature etc at many heights
– Report by pressure levels
• Mandatory and Significant Pressure Levels
– Up to ~100mb level (~16 km). 1mb = 100Pa
• Do include all levels in modeling (Mand & Sigs)
• 1990-present, past data available by order
– Integrated Global Radiosonde Archive (IGRA) 
from NCEI not supported

heading: Where are the data / • One met stations may has several IDs
text:
Where are the data
• One met stations may has several IDs
– Station call sign (e.g. KMCO)
– US Air Force ID (e.g. 722050)
– WBAN (Weather-Bureau-Army-Navy) ID (e.g. 12815)
– WMO (World Meteorological Organization) ID
• Surface, ISHD hourly data
– TD-3505 format
– Most up to date full ISHD inventory: 
ftp://ftp.ncdc.noaa.gov/pub/data/noaa/isd-history.csv
– Explore data at: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/search/data-
search/global-hourly
• Find a station: use “Map View”
• Name format: USAF ID + “-” + WBAN ID + “-” + Year
• Check if format is correct!

heading: Where are the data / • Surface, 1-min ASOS data
text:
Where are the data
• Surface, 1-min ASOS data
– TD-6405 format
– ftp://ftp.ncdc.noaa.gov/pub/data/asos-onemin/
– Look for folders  start with 6405
– File format: 6405 + 0 + station call sign + YYYY + MM
– To find a station near your study area:
• https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/weather/asos/
• Look for only ASOS stations
• Upper air sounding data
– TD-6201 is outdated! Use FSL format
– Download from: https://ruc.noaa.gov/raobs/
– 1990-present, past data available by order

heading: Stage 1 / • Extract and QA raw, archived observations
text:
Stage 1
• Extract and QA raw, archived observations
– Surface, upper air, and on-site data
• Allowable pathways
– JOB: messages and reports
– SURFACE: process surface data
– UPPERAIR: process upper air data
– ONSITE: process on-site data

heading: Stage 1 Pathway: JOB / • Most useful Keywords:
text:
Stage 1 Pathway: JOB
• Most useful Keywords:
– MESSAGES: log file
• Format: MESSAGES log_file_name
– REPORT: optional, summary report
• Format: REPORT summary_file_name
• Example
JOB
MESSAGES     TestRun.MSG
REPORT          TestRun.RPT

heading: Stage 1 Pathway: SURFACE / • Most useful Keywords:
text:
Stage 1 Pathway: SURFACE
• Most useful Keywords:
– DATA: Archived surface data name and format
• Format: DATA file_name file_format
– EXTRACT: Name of file contains all extracted data
• Format: EXTRACT extracted_file_name
– QAOUT: Name of file contained QA’ed data
• Format: QAOUT qa_data_filename
– You can choose not to use either all data record, or 
only QA’ed data for later calculation

heading: Stage 1 Pathway: SURFACE / • Most useful Keywords:
text:
Stage 1 Pathway: SURFACE
• Most useful Keywords:
– LOCATION: coordinates of surface station
• Format: LOCATION site_id lat lon [timeadjust] [elevation]
• Lat and lon can be reverse, need to be positive numbers
• Timeadjust and elevation (meters) are optional
• ISHD is reported in GMT time, all others in local time
– Thus timeadjust is set to 0 for data other than ISHD
• Timeadjust is reverse of standard timezone #
– Specify 5 for eastern US (UTC-5), not daylight time
– XDATES: Range of date to extract
• Format: XDATES YB/MB/DB YE/ME/DE
– 4 digits year, 2 or 1 digits month and day
– 2 digits year no longer works

heading: Stage 1 Pathway: SURFACE / • Example
text:
Stage 1 Pathway: SURFACE
• Example
SURFACE
DATA 722050-12815-2022 ISHD
EXTRACT        MCO_2022_Extract.dat
QAOUT MCO_2022_QAout.dat
LOCATION       722050 28.434N 81.325W 5 0
XDATES           2022/1/1 2022/12/31
Avoid using “tab” in input file

heading: Stage 1 Pathway: UPPERAIR / • Most useful Keywords:
text:
Stage 1 Pathway: UPPERAIR
• Most useful Keywords:
– DATA: Archived upper air data name and format
• Format: DATA file_name file_format
– EXTRACT: Name of file contains all extracted data
• Format: EXTRACT extracted_file_name
– QAOUT: Name of file contained QA’ed data
• Format: QAOUT qa_data_filename

heading: Stage 1 Pathway: UPPERAIR / • Most useful Keywords:
text:
Stage 1 Pathway: UPPERAIR
• Most useful Keywords:
– LOCATION: coordinates of upper air station
• Format: LOCATION site_id lat lon timeadjust
• Lat and lon can be reverse, need to be positive numbers
• Timeadjust is not optional
• All upper air data reported in GMT time
• Timeadjust is reverse of standard timezone #
– Specify 5 for eastern US (UTC-5), not daylight time
– XDATES: Range of date to extract
• Format: XDATES YB/MB/DB YE/ME/DE
– 4 digits year, 2 or 1 digits month and day
– 2 digits year no longer works

heading: Stage 2 / • Using stage 1 data, calculate
text:
Stage 2
• Using stage 1 data, calculate 
meteorological parameters for AERMOD
• Combined past stage 2 & 3
• Allowable pathways
– JOB: messages and reports
– SURFACE: specific stage 1 surface data
– UPPERAIR: specific stage 1 upper air data

heading: Stage 2 / • JOB pathway
text:
Stage 2
• JOB pathway
– MESSAGES: log file
– REPORT: optional, summary report
• SURFACE pathway
– QAOUT: QA’ed, or not QA’ed, surface data
– ASOS1MIN: AERMINUTE processed ASOS data
• UPPERAIR pathway
– QAOUT: Similar with SURFACE

heading: Stage 3 pathway: METPREP / • METPREP pathway
text:
Stage 3 pathway: METPREP
• METPREP pathway
– DATA: stage 2 merged file
– XDATES: time range of processing
– OUTPUT: output file for surface data
– PROFILE: output file for profile (upper air) data
– Specify surface characteristics
• FREQ_SECT, SECTOR, and SITE_CHAR
• Can copy and paste output from AERSURFACE
• Can spatially vary by sector (up to 12)
• Can Temporally vary by season/month
• Need two sets data if both on-site and NWS data used

heading: Stage 3 pathway: METPREP / • METPREP pathway
text:
Stage 3 pathway: METPREP
• METPREP pathway
– Can specify spatially varying surface characteristics
– More detail later in AERSURFACE
• FREQ_SECT: spatial & temporal changing patterns
– Format: FREQ_SECT frequency #sectors
– Frequency can be: ANNUAL, SEASONAL, or MONTHLY
– #sectors: how many zones revolving around the center (12 max)
• SECTOR: define spatial zones revolving around center
– Format: SECTOR sector_index beginning_direction ending_direction
• SITE_CHAR: provide surface characteristics data
– Format: SITE_CHAR freq_idx sector_idx albedo Bowen roughness
– freq_idx: # frequency in FREQ_SECT
– sector_idx: # sector in SECTOR

heading: Stage 3 pathway: METPREP / • METPREP pathway
text:
Stage 3 pathway: METPREP
• METPREP pathway
– NWS_HGT: specify height of surface instrument
• Format: NWS_HGT WIND height
• Height is in meters
– METHOD: specify detailed processing method
• Format: METHOD variable option
• Several combinations available
• METHOD WIND_DIR NORAND
– Do not modify current wind direction
• METHOD WIND_DIR RANDOM
– Randomly +/- a few degrees to wind direction
– NWS reports wind direction in nearest 10 degrees

heading: Stage 3 pathway: METPREP / • METPREP pathway
text:
Stage 3 pathway: METPREP
• METPREP pathway
– METHOD (continue)
• METHOD REFLEVEL SUBNWS
– When on-site data used, but missing for certain hours, 
substitute missing on-site data with NWS data
– When only NWS data used, this needs to be in inputs
• METHOD STABLEBL ADJ_U*
– Adjust U* at low wind speed (sounds familiar?)
– METHOD also has several other options, but we will 
skip them here. Check section 4.7.6 of AERMET user 
guide

heading: Stage 2 example input / JOB
text:
Stage 2 example input
JOB
MESSAGES  TestRun_3.MSG
REPORT        TestRun_3.RPT
SURFACE
QAOUT    MCO_2022_QAout.dat 
UPPERAIR
QAOUT    UA_2022_QAout_FSL_knot.dat
METPREP
XDATES         2022/1/1  2022/12/31
METHOD        REFLEVEL  SUBNWS
METHOD        WIND_DIR  RANDOM
NWS_HGT      WIND     10
OUTPUT         ORLANDO.SFC
PROFILE        ORLANDO.PFL
FREQ_SECT  ANNUAL 1
SECTOR        1   0  360
SITE_CHAR   1   1  0.2  1  0.5

AERMINUTE
• AERMINUTE uses an input file (not interactive)
• The input file requires at least four sections
– STARTEND: start and end month of data processing
– IFWGROUP: if/when this station measures ice free wind (IFW)
• Ice affect cup and vane sensors, not heated sonic anemometers
• Installation date of IFW wind instrument:
– https://www.weather.gov/media/asos/ASOS%20Implementation/IFW_stat.pdf
– DATAFILE: list of input data files
• Starts with “DATAFILE STARTING”, end with “DATAFILE FINISHED”
• List all 1-min ASOS data files
– OUTFILES: list of output data files
• Starts with “OUTFILES STARTING”, end with “OUTFILES FINISHED”
• HOURFILE: name of output hourly data for AERMET

output data are also available:
– aerminute.log: a log file
– good_records.dat: input data passed QA/QC
– bad_records.dat: input data failed QA/QC
– check_records.dat: input data seems 
suspicious (thus not used), but just might be

heading: Other options / • AERMINUTE also has several other options available
text:
Other options
• AERMINUTE also has several other options available
– Include 5-min ASOS data
– Compare averaged data with regular hourly measurement data
• And output comparison results to a file
• This is because ASOS data commonly contains substantially more calm 
record (wind speed < 1 m/s) than regular hourly data, so it’s worth to 
compare the two
– Provide a summary file for each hour
